\chapter{Grey, Pink And Dark}
\label{ch:gris-y-rosa}
\hlchaptermodality{372}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say gris, rosa, oscuro, pálido and suave, and pick out which thing I mean by how it looks and how it feels.}

Complete ES-C372-suave: pick out which thing you mean by how it looks and how it feels.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[gris]{gris — a colour that came in from the north}

\label{lesson:ES-C372-gris}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{slow}, then \emph{sweet}. (\emph{Lento}; \emph{dulce}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item negro, blanco — the two this one sits between.
  \item la nube — the thing it describes most often.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{GRIS}, one beat. The \emph{g} is hard, the \emph{r} is a single tap, and the \emph{s} at the end stays crisp. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{gris} — \textquotedblleft{}grey.\textquotedblright{}

Most Spanish colour words come down from Latin. This one does not.

\emph{Gris} is \textbf{Germanic}, and it walked into Spanish sideways — through the Romance languages to the north, along the routes that carried furs and cloth. One of its earliest Spanish appearances is in a thirteenth-century inventory, describing a fur.

English \textbf{grey} is a cousin, not a twin. The two go back to two different Germanic stems that happen to mean the same thing — so \emph{gris} and \emph{grey} are family, but they are not the same word wearing two spellings.

The Germanic word left tracks all over English, and they are easy to spot once you know what you are spotting:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{grizzled} — greying, through French \emph{grisel};
  \item \textbf{grisaille} — a painting done entirely in greys, so that it imitates stone;
  \item \textbf{ambergris} — the waxy substance from a whale, used in perfume. The name is French \emph{ambre gris}, \textbf{grey amber}, distinguishing it from \emph{ambre jaune}, the yellow amber that is fossil resin. People have offered prettier stories for that word — amber grease, amber of Greece — and they are inventions.
\end{itemize}

A colour word that took a trade route, arriving with the goods it described.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe an overcast day: \emph{el cielo está gris}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{gris}
  \item \emph{muy gris}
  \item \emph{el cielo está gris}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did \emph{gris} come from Latin? (No — it is a Germanic word taken in through Spanish's northern neighbours.) And what does \emph{ambergris} mean? (Grey amber.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rosa]{rosa — a flower Latin borrowed, and a herb that is not one}

\label{lesson:ES-C372-rosa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{sweet}, then \emph{grey}. (\emph{Dulce}; \emph{gris}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la flor — the class the flower belongs to.
  \item rojo — the colour this one is a pale version of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RO-sa}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{r} at the start of a word is rolled, and the \emph{s} between vowels stays crisp. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{rosa} — \textquotedblleft{}pink,\textquotedblright{} and also \textquotedblleft{}the rose.\textquotedblright{}

Spanish does the same thing English does with \emph{orange}: one word for the flower and for the shade it comes in.

Latin \textbf{rosa} looks like the most Latin word imaginable, and Latin did not make it. The rose came from the east and its name came with it — most likely through a dialect form of Greek \textbf{rhódon}, and behind the Greek an Iranian word. The route has a hole in it: nobody has explained where the Latin \emph{s} came from, when Greek has a \emph{d}. So the borrowing is certain and the road it took is not.

The Greek side of that same loan is standing in English already: \textbf{rhododendron}, the rose tree.

And now the trap, which is one of the finest in English. \textbf{Rosemary} has nothing to do with a rose, and nothing to do with Mary.

It is Latin \textbf{rōs marīnus} — \textbf{sea dew}. English speakers who had never met \emph{rōs} or \emph{marīnus} heard two words they did know, and pulled the spelling across to fit. The plant kept the sound and lost the sense.

That is folk etymology working exactly as it always works: not by lying, but by making a strange word comfortable. Every time you write \emph{rosemary} you are writing down somebody's guess from several centuries ago.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now name a colour and a flower at once: \emph{rosa}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{rosa}
  \item \emph{una flor rosa}
  \item \emph{la casa es rosa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Did Latin build the word \emph{rosa} or borrow it? (Borrow it, from the east.) And what does \emph{rosemary} actually mean? (Sea dew — \emph{rōs marīnus}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[oscuro]{oscuro — a word split down the middle by scholars}

\label{lesson:ES-C372-oscuro}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{grey}, then \emph{pink}. (\emph{Gris}; \emph{rosa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la luz — what it is the absence of.
  \item la noche — when there is most of it.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{os-CU-ro}, three beats with the weight on the second. The \emph{sc} is an \emph{s} against a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{r} is a single tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{oscuro} — \textquotedblleft{}dark.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{obscūrus}, and English borrowed it whole as \textbf{obscure} — which still carries the darkness under its modern sense. An obscure passage is one you cannot see into.

Splitting the word is easy: \textbf{ob-}, a common Latin prefix, plus a second piece that means dark.

Saying where that second piece came from is not easy at all, and this lesson is here to show you a live disagreement rather than a settled answer.

The older reference books attach it to an ancient root meaning \textbf{to cover}, and draw in a wide family of English words on the strength of it. The standard modern dictionary of Latin origins rejects that and attaches it instead to a root meaning \textbf{dark} outright — pointing out that \textquotedblleft{}cover\textquotedblright{} makes poor sense with the prefix, and listing none of that family. A third scholar has proposed cutting the word at a different point altogether.

So: the meaning is certain, the prefix is certain, and the ancestry is open. The honest thing is to hand you the word and the argument, rather than one book's answer dressed up as the answer.

One relative that is not in doubt. Italian \textbf{chiaroscuro} is \emph{chiaro} plus \emph{scuro}, bright plus dark — the painter's term for a scene lit by one small source, all highlight and shadow with little in between.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe a room or a colour: \emph{muy oscuro}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{oscuro}
  \item \emph{muy oscuro}
  \item \emph{la noche es oscura}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{obscūrus}? (\emph{Ob-} and a piece meaning dark.) And what does \emph{chiaroscuro} name? (Bright and dark together — the painter's word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pálido]{pálido — one Latin word, arriving twice}

\label{lesson:ES-C372-palido}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{pink}, then \emph{dark}. (\emph{Rosa}; \emph{oscuro}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cara — where you notice it first.
  \item el color — what it is a shortage of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{PÁ-li-do}, three beats with the weight on the \textbf{first}, which is why the accent is written: the ordinary place for it would be the second. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pálido} — \textquotedblleft{}pale.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{pallidus}, from the verb \textbf{pallēre}, to be pale. English has this word twice over, and the pair is worth setting side by side because it shows what the two roads do to a word:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{pale} came through Old French. Passing through a spoken language wore it down to one syllable and took the double \emph{l} out;
  \item \textbf{pallid} was taken straight off the written Latin. It kept both \emph{l}'s and the ending, and it kept a bookish feel that \emph{pale} has lost.
\end{itemize}

Same Latin adjective, several centuries apart, and English uses them differently without anybody deciding to.

A third relative hides its face. To \textbf{appall} is the same family through French: to make somebody go pale. An appalling thing is one that drains the colour out of a face, which is a much more physical word than its everyday use suggests.

And the inherited Germanic cousin — never borrowed, come down the other line — is \textbf{fallow}: the dull yellowish brown of a fallow deer, or of a field left unsown. Pale and fallow meet only far back, at the reconstructed level, but they meet.

One neighbour to leave alone: \textbf{la palabra}, a word, is nothing to do with any of this. It comes from Greek \emph{parabolē} with two of its letters swapped on the way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe someone who does not look well: \emph{está pálido}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pálido}
  \item \emph{muy pálido}
  \item \emph{está pálido}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \emph{pale} and \emph{pallid} came through French? (\emph{Pale}.) And what does it mean to appall somebody, literally? (To make them go pale.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[suave]{suave — the same word as sweet}

\label{lesson:ES-C372-suave}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{dark}, then \emph{pale}. (\emph{Oscuro}; \emph{pálido}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la piel — the first thing you call \emph{suave}.
  \item la manta — the second.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SUA-ve}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{ua} is one glide, and the \emph{v} is the same soft sound as a Spanish \emph{b}. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{suave} — \textquotedblleft{}smooth, soft, gentle.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{suāvis} meant agreeable to the senses — pleasant to taste, to touch, to hear.

English \textbf{sweet} is the same word. Not a translation of it: the same ancient root, come down the Germanic line instead of the Latin one, changing sound by sound until nothing recognisable was left on the surface. \emph{Suave} and \emph{sweet} are twins raised in different houses.

Latin built a verb on that root too: \textbf{suādēre}, to advise, to urge. Which means \textbf{persuade} is \emph{per-} plus that verb — to make a thing thoroughly \textbf{sweet} to somebody. You do not persuade a person by proving them wrong; the word says you persuade them by making your position pleasant to accept. And \textbf{dissuade} is the same move in reverse.

\textbf{Assuage} belongs here as well, arriving through French: to sweeten a grief until it can be borne.

English also borrowed \textbf{suave} itself, straight off the Latin in the fifteenth century. Its modern sense — smooth manners, a shade too smooth — came later, under French influence, and is the language's own judgement rather than anything the Romans put there.

Further back still, Greek \emph{hēdys}, sweet, belongs to the same root — and \textbf{hedonism} is built on it. Sweetness as a philosophy.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can now describe how something feels: \emph{muy suave}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{suave}
  \item \emph{muy suave}
  \item \emph{la manta es suave}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which everyday English word is the inherited cousin of \emph{suave}? (\emph{Sweet}.) And what does \emph{persuade} say, taken apart? (To make a thing sweet to somebody.)
\end{tcolorbox}
